title: Cinema of China
wiki_lead: The cinema of China is the filmmaking and film industry of mainland China, one of three distinct historical threads of Chinese-language cinema together with the cinema of Hong Kong and the cinema of Taiwan. China is the home of the largest movie and drama production complex and film studios in the world, the Oriental Movie Metropolis and Hengdian World Studios. In 2012 the country became the second-largest market in the world by box office receipts behind only the United States. In 2016 the gross box office in China was CN¥45.71 billion (US$6.58 billion). China has also become a major hub of business for Hollywood studios.

The cinema of China is the filmmaking and film industry of mainland China, one of three distinct historical threads of Chinese-language cinema together with the cinema of Hong Kong and the cinema of Taiwan. China is the home of the largest movie and drama production complex and film studios in the world, the Oriental Movie Metropolis and Hengdian World Studios. In 2012 the country became the second-largest market in the world by box office receipts behind only the United States. In 2016 the gross box office in China was CN¥45.71 billion (US$6.58 billion). China has also become a major hub of business for Hollywood studios.


History


Beginnings
While early accounts traditionally date the introduction of cinema to China to an anonymous variety show in August 1896 at Shanghai's Xu Garden teahouse, archival newspaper research by Dr Yongchun Fu demonstrates that this event was a magic lantern exhibition projecting still glass slides (yingxi). The historical record confirms that the first true motion picture exhibition in China occurred on May 22, 1897, when itinerant showman Harry Welby Cook projected celluloid film strips using Edison's Animatoscope at the Astor House Hotel in Shanghai. Later that summer Cook also produced China's earliest localized actualities by filming local bicycle riders and swimming baths before expanding his commercial film circuit north to Tianjin and Beijing.
Chinese-made short melodrama and comedy films began emerging in 1913. In 1913 the first independent Chinese screenplay, The Difficult Couple, was filmed in Shanghai by Zheng Zhengqiu and Zhang Shichuan.  Zhang Shichuan then set up the first Chinese-owned film production company in 1916. The first full-length feature film was Yan Ruisheng (閻瑞生), released in 1921, which was a docudrama about the killing of a Shanghai courtesan.
Chinese film production developed significantly in the 1920s. During this time film technicians from the United States trained Chinese technicians in Shanghai, and American influence continued to be felt there for the next two decades. Since film was still in its earliest stages of development, most Chinese silent films were only comic skits or operatic shorts, and training was minimal in technical aspects due to this being a period of experimental films. Throughout the 1920s and 1930s filmmaking in China was largely done by film studios and there was comparatively little small scale filmmaking.
Upscale movie theaters in China had contracts which required them to exclusively show Hollywood films, and thus as of the late 1920s, Hollywood films accounted for 90% of screen time in Chinese theaters.
After trials and errors China was able to draw inspiration from its traditional values and began producing martial arts films, with the first being Burning of Red Lotus Temple (1928). Burning of Red Lotus Temple was so successful at the box office, the Star Motion Pictures (Mingxing) production company later filmed 18 sequels, marking the beginning of China's esteemed martial arts film genre. Many imitators followed, including U. Lien (Youlian) Studio's Red Heroine (1929), which is still extant. It was during this period that some of the more important production companies first came into being, notably Mingxing and the Shaw brothers' Tianyi ("Unique"). Mingxing, founded by Zheng Zhengqiu and Zhang Shichuan in 1922, initially focused on comic shorts, including the oldest surviving complete Chinese film Laborer's Love (1922), but soon shifted to feature-length films and family dramas such as Orphan Rescues Grandfather (1923). Meanwhile Tianyi moved their model toward folklore dramas and also pushed into foreign markets; their film White Snake (1926) proved a typical example of their success in the Chinese communities of Southeast Asia. In 1931 the first Chinese sound film Sing-Song Girl Red Peony was made, the product of a cooperation between the Mingxing Film Company's image production and Pathé Frères' sound technology. grok_lead: The Cinema of China refers to the motion picture industry operating within the People's Republic of China, which traces its origins to the screening of foreign films in 1896 and the production of the first domestic feature, Dingjun Mountain, in 1905. Centered initially in Shanghai, the industry flourished in the 1930s with socially conscious narratives and commercial successes amid urban modernity, only to face disruption from Japanese invasion and civil war. Following the 1949 communist victory, film production was nationalized under the Chinese Communist Party, prioritizing ideological propaganda and socialist realism, with output nearly ceasing during the Cultural Revolution (1966â1976) due to political purges. Post-1978 economic reforms spurred revival, enabling the emergence of the Fifth Generation directorsâsuch as Zhang Yimou and Chen Kaige âwhose visually striking films like Red Sorghum (1987) and Farewell My Concubine (1993) garnered international acclaim and awards, including Palme d'Or nominations at Cannes, while subtly critiquing historical traumas within permitted bounds. By the 2000s, market liberalization and state investment propelled commercial blockbusters, with domestic productions dominating the box office, which peaked at over 64 billion yuan in 2019 before declining to 42.5 billion yuan in 2024 amid economic slowdowns and streaming competition, though early 2026 earnings surpassed 2 billion yuan by February, driven by domestic productions and Spring Festival anticipation, signaling a potential rebound. Yet this growth occurs under stringent censorship enforced by the National Radio and Television Administration, which mandates pre-approval and prohibits content deemed subversive, supernatural, or critical of the Party, often compelling self-censorship to align with official narratives and limiting artistic freedom. Internationally, select films like Zhang Yimou's Hero (2002) have achieved Oscar nominations and global appeal through martial arts spectacle and historical epics, though broader recognition remains hampered by domestic controls and geopolitical sensitivities. The industry's dual roleâas a tool for cultural soft power and a profit-driven enterpriseâhighlights tensions between commercial ambition and authoritarian oversight, with recent indie voices like Jia Zhangke navigating underground circuits to depict contemporary social realities.
